# 4. DISCUSSION

The acoustic-trawl survey (ATS) datasets recovered through this project comprise a substantial archive of limnetic fish-monitoring information collected from British Columbia lakes between 1977 and 2007. Recovery and standardization of these records have improved accessibility to historical acoustic-target, trawl-biosampling, and associated metadata records that were previously distributed across multiple legacy formats. The resulting datasets provide information on survey effort, fish-like target (FLT) observations, trawl catches, species composition, and biological measurements collected over multiple decades and across a broad geographic range.

## 4.1. Data Rescue Outcomes

The primary objective of this project was to recover, document, and publish historical ATS datasets. A total of 123,819 acoustic FLT records and 177,541 trawl biosampling records were recovered, quality-controlled, and verified. In addition, associated metadata describing survey effort, acoustic equipment, lake physical characteristics, and trawl sampling activities were assembled from available source files and supporting documentation.

The rescue process highlighted the value of preserving supporting metadata alongside biological observations. Much of the interpretation of historical records depended upon information contained within legacy file structures, lookup tables, technical reports, and other documentation. Without these supporting materials, interpretation of some dataset fields would have been difficult or impossible.

## 4.2. Dataset Completeness and Availability

The datasets described in this report represent the records that could be located and recovered during the present data-rescue initiative. They should not be considered a complete inventory of all information collected during the ATS program. Additional records may remain in spreadsheets, archived databases, technical reports, field forms, laboratory records, or other historical sources that were outside the scope of, or not available during, this project. 

Additional challenges were encountered during data rescue and standardization. Scale books and scale book identification numbers were not standardized, making it difficult to determine the meaning of some codes and their correspondence to specific sampling events or records. Fish length and weight measurements were also recorded using different units (cm/mm and g/mg, respectively), requiring careful examination and standardization to ensure data accuracy. Despite these efforts, some values may remain unconverted or incorrectly recorded. Missing data represent another important limitation, including possibly undetected gaps within years for which rescued data were otherwise available. This issue was particularly evident in the trawl dataset, for which no data could be recovered yet for the period from 2000 to 2007. Consequently, data availability and completeness should be evaluated before conducting analyses, particularly those requiring consistent temporal coverage or comparisons among sampling periods.

Consequently, apparent absences within the rescued datasets should be interpreted cautiously. Missing records may reflect incomplete historical archives, unavailable source files, or unresolved data-recovery issues rather than the absence of field sampling. Future recovery efforts may identify additional ATS records and supporting documentation that could further improve the completeness of the published datasets.

## 4.3. Survey Coverage and Comparability

Survey effort varied considerably among lakes and ATS years. Several lakes – referred to as “key lakes” – received repeated sampling over long periods, whereas many others were surveyed intermittently or for relatively short durations. The Results section also demonstrates substantial variation in survey timing and biological sampling among lakes and years. The ATS monitoring program was conducted over an extended period, during which different field crews were involved in data collection, using different hydroacoustic equipment. Furthermore, the sampling methodology was developed and modified throughout the implementation of the program, potentially introducing temporal differences in sampling procedures and limiting direct comparisons among years. The best sources of methods for a given field season or individual lake are the historical reports cited throughout, together with information contained in the metadata associated with the recovered records; even so, these may not comprise a complete record of methods. Additionally, SiRE holds summary trip report (STR) files that contain additional metadata; these may be made more widely available in the future.

These methodological and consistency differences should be considered when comparing observations among lakes or ATS years. Variability in survey coverage may influence summary statistics and visualizations presented in this report. Consequently, the figures and tables presented here are intended primarily to describe dataset characteristics and data availability rather than to support formal assessments of long-term population trends.

The March 31/April 1 cut-off may not apply to all Sockeye nursery lakes; the analyst should review published data, and technical and manuscript reports in the Canadian Reports of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences series (available at DFO libraries, https://science-libraries.canada.ca/eng/fisheries-oceans), to determine the outmigration dates, and the resulting ATS years, for individual lakes of interest. 


## 4.4. Interpretation of Acoustic Target Data

The acoustic dataset contains records of fish-like targets detected during hydroacoustic surveys. These observations provide information on the distribution and relative abundance of acoustic targets within surveyed lakes; however, FLT observations should not be interpreted as direct measurements of fish abundance without additional analytical assumptions and scaling procedures.

An additional consideration is the limited representation of fish abundance in our dataset in near-surface waters. Historical hydroacoustic equipment was unable to reliably detect fish within approximately the upper 2 m of the water column because of near-surface interference, vessel movement, and transducer limitations. As a result, acoustic observations are concentrated in deeper strata. Surface trawl sampling was used in some surveys to sample fish occupying shallow habitats, but coverage varied among lakes and ATS years.

## 4.5. Species Composition and Size Considerations

All species composition information within the ATS datasets originates from trawl biosampling records. Species proportions recorded in some acoustic source files were derived from trawl observations and applied to acoustic survey transect depth strata at higher spatial resolution than supported by the trawl sampling efforts. Proportions in the acoustic data should therefore be interpreted as supporting metadata rather than independent acoustic observations.

Users should also be aware that juvenile Sockeye Salmon and Kokanee were not consistently distinguished in all lakes or years, given the unavailability of ready DNA analyses at that time. Consequently, Sockeye Salmon records almost certainly include some Kokanee in systems where both ecotypes were present. Investigators conducting lake-specific analyses should consider local biological and stock information when interpreting species composition results.

It should also be noted that larger fish would be underrepresented in trawl catches due to their greater ability to evade the net. This affects the ability of the trawl to catch species that were typically larger than juvenile Sockeye Salmon, and also larger age classes of Sockeye Salmon and Kokanee (@hyattAcousticTrawlBased2000, Fig. 7).

## 4.6. Biological Measurements and Data Quality

The trawl biosampling dataset contains a substantial amount of biological information, including species identifications, fish lengths, weights, ages, and life-stage information. Quality-control procedures employed here identified a small number of anomalous observations and incomplete records. Where possible, these records were retained and documented rather than removed from the cleaned dataset in order to preserve transparency and maintain consistency with original source materials.

As with many historical datasets, some records contain missing values, errors, incomplete species information, or measurements that warrant additional review before use in specific analyses. Users are encouraged to review accompanying metadata and data-quality flags prior to undertaking detailed biological analyses.

## 4.7. Future Applications

The rescued ATS datasets provide opportunities for future investigations of juvenile salmon ecology, nursery-lake productivity, fish community structure, and long-term environmental change. The availability of both acoustic and trawl datasets, together with supporting metadata, allow historical observations to be revisited using contemporary analytical methods and statistical approaches.

Future work could focus on identifying and recovering additional ATS records, integrating historical and contemporary monitoring datasets, and developing standardized indicators derived from long-term ATS observations. Specifically, this will entail recovery of trawl data and echosounder data that may still be missing from the current data rescue, and especially trawl data for all ATS lakes for the years 2000-2007, as well as any datasets in SiRE Program storage for the limited number of study lakes surveyed post-2007. Continued preservation and documentation of supporting metadata will further increase the utility of these datasets for research and management applications.

Several of the ATS lakes, including those identified as key study lakes in this report, were monitored repeatedly over extended periods and contain comparatively complete acoustic, trawl, and biological records. These systems may provide opportunities for development and evaluation of a Sockeye Salmon indicator-stock framework, whereby trends observed in a limited number of well-monitored nursery lakes could be used to infer broader patterns in productivity, survival, or environmental conditions within less intensively monitored watersheds nearby. The long-term and multi-decadal nature of the ATS datasets provides a valuable foundation for exploring the suitability of such indicator systems and evaluating the degree to which key study lakes represent regional patterns in juvenile Sockeye Salmon production. However, the extent to which individual key lakes are representative of broader regional dynamics would require additional investigation.

# 5. CONCLUSIONS

This project successfully recovered and documented a substantial portion of the historical ATS archive. Although limitations associated with data availability, survey coverage, species identification, and historical documentation should be considered when interpreting the datasets, the rescued records represent an important source of information on British Columbia Sockeye Salmon nursery lakes and associated fish communities. Publication of these datasets and supporting metadata preserves their long-term value and provides a foundation for future scientific, management, and data-recovery activities, particularly in the context of understanding long-term changes in lake ecosystems and fish populations. In addition to preserving historical observations, publication of these datasets substantially reduces the risk of future data loss by consolidating records, metadata, documentation, and processing workflows into publicly accessible and reproducible data products.
